description:
We are a motivated team passionate about space, technology and data. Our goal is to bring the story of the rovers, landers and objects left on the Moon and Mars back to life through an interactive and engaging experience.
We believe that every piece of equipment left behind has a story worth telling, and we want to share it in a creative and accessible way.
summary:
Lunar Explorer is an interactive 3D web experience that brings NASA’s forgotten Moon hardware back to life for younger audiences and space enthusiasts.

Since the 1960s, NASA has left landers, rovers and science instruments on the Moon. Yet young people mostly hear about active missions, and the stories of these machines stay buried in technical catalogues. Our project answers one question: how can we turn NASA’s open data about objects left on the Moon into an interactive story that helps people understand how these machines worked and what they taught us?

Users orbit a 3D Moon built from NASA imagery and elevation data, choose an Apollo mission (11, 15 or 17), and fly down to its real landing site. There, they drive a rover to discover objects placed at their real positions from LROC data, and inspect official NASA 3D models and photos. An illustrated book, “How NASA reached the Moon”, tells the journey in seven chapters. Every position and caption comes from NASA sources.

Lunar Explorer turns dense data into an adventure, so these machines stay abandoned, but not forgotten.
details:
WHAT LUNAR EXPLORER DOES

Lunar Explorer is an interactive 3D web application that tells the story of the real objects humanity left on the Moon. It is designed for younger audiences and space enthusiasts who usually only hear about active missions.

Users start by orbiting a 3D Moon. They choose an Apollo mission (Apollo 11, 15 or 17) and a cinematic flight takes them down to the real landing site. There, they drive a rover across the surface to discover the objects the astronauts left behind. Each discovered object opens an inspection screen with the official NASA 3D model, NASA photographs with their original captions, and sourced mission information. An illustrated interactive book, "How NASA reached the Moon", tells the full journey in 7 chapters and 22 animated steps, with a simple or detailed reading mode.

Our guiding question: how can we turn NASA's open data about objects left on the Moon into an interactive story that helps people understand how these machines worked and what they taught us?

HOW IT WORKS – KEY TECHNICAL INNOVATIONS

- Real positions from LROC: object positions come word-for-word from the official LROC "Anthropogenic Objects" table. A dedicated import script regenerates the dataset from the original file.

- A dataset builder with confidence ratings: objects are classified by category, and each position gets a reliability rating, so users know how precise a location is.

- Server-side source checks: the backend verifies that every source and research reference used in the book exists before serving it. Landing coordinates always come from LROC, never from free text.

- 3D Moon from NASA data: the orbital globe uses the NASA SVS colour map and LOLA elevation data (Globe.gl).

- Real-direction surface scenes: in the Three.js landing-site scene, the Lunar Module descent stage is the origin, and every object keeps its real direction from the lander. Distances are shortened for gameplay, and this is clearly stated.

- Official NASA 3D models: a reusable WebGL viewer lets users rotate, zoom and highlight parts, with an assembly animation of the Lunar Modules Eagle, Falcon and Challenger.

- Flexible, tested backend: a Node.js + Express REST API runs on bundled JSON by default, or on PostgreSQL + PostGIS for spatial queries. It is covered by 12 automated API tests.

- Honest by design: everything illustrative (terrain, reconstructed models, book drawings) is labelled as such.

Technology stack: React, Vite, Three.js and Globe.gl (frontend); Node.js and Express (backend); JSON or PostgreSQL + PostGIS (data); LROC, NASA SVS / LOLA, NASA 3D Resources and the NASA Image and Video Library (NASA data).

BUSINESS MODEL INTEGRATION

Lunar Explorer is built as a free educational tool, with a model that keeps it free for learners:

- Free core for students and the public: the full experience stays free and runs in a browser, with no installation.

- Schools and teachers: classroom packs (lesson guides, quizzes, progress tracking) offered to schools and education programs.

- Museums and planetariums: white-label or kiosk versions for exhibitions about space exploration.

- Partnerships and grants: science outreach grants and partnerships with space agencies, universities, science foundations and sponsors who support STEM education.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

Benefits:

- For students: learn space history by exploring and playing, with accurate, sourced facts.

- For teachers: a free, ready-to-use and verifiable tool for science and history classes.

- For NASA's heritage: these objects stay remembered as monuments of exploration, not forgotten hardware.

Goals:

- Make NASA's lunar heritage engaging and accessible to younger audiences.

- Show the link between the engineering of each machine and the science it made possible.

- Pilot the tool in schools and measure learning with a quiz before and after use.

- Extend the experience to Mars with the same architecture (HiRISE data).

PRESENTING LUNAR EXPLORER RESULTS

During the hackathon, our team of four delivered a working prototype:

- A 3D orbital Moon built from NASA SVS and LOLA data.

- Three explorable Apollo landing sites (Apollo 11, 15 and 17), with a drivable rover, a mini-map, mission objectives and saved progress.

- Objects placed from the official LROC table, with a confidence rating for each position.

- An object inspection screen with official NASA 3D models, NASA photographs and a Lunar Module assembly animation.

- An interactive book of 7 chapters and 22 animated steps.

- A REST API with 12 passing tests, running on JSON or PostgreSQL + PostGIS.

Supporting analyses:

- TELOS feasibility study: a score of 4.28 / 5, robust across 10,000 simulations.

- Multicriteria index (LHI): used to rank which objects to feature. The Apollo 11 laser reflector comes first; it is still used by scientists today.

- Market estimate: based on official data (9.22 million students in Morocco, 92.3% of the population online), with a Monte Carlo projection of about a 79% probability of passing 10,000 users in the first year. These figures are projections based on our assumptions.

BUSINESS MODEL, PROFITABILITY & SUSTAINABILITY

- Low costs: the frontend can be hosted as a static site and the API is lightweight. NASA data and 3D models are free to use with credit, so running costs stay very low.

- Revenue sources (projected): classroom packs for schools, museum and planetarium licences, sponsorships and education grants. The student version stays free.

- Sustainability: an automated data pipeline (re-import from LROC, server-side checks, tests) keeps the content easy to maintain. New missions or Mars sites can be added without rebuilding the app.

- Next steps: a pilot in 2 to 3 schools, partnerships with astronomy associations, and the Mars extension.

Abandoned, but not forgotten.
